title: Testing a Claim about a Mean
short: Carry out a one-sample t test.

blocks.html: A test for a mean follows the same steps as a test for a proportion, with the t distribution from confidence intervals for a mean in place of z.

To test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$: $$t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}, \quad df = n - 1.$$ The p-value is the area beyond t under the t curve, in the direction of $H_a$. Conditions: a random sample, and a roughly normal population or a large sample.

If $H_0$ is true, $\bar{x}$ varies around $\mu_0$ with standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. We estimate that with $s/\sqrt{n}$, which makes the standardized statistic follow a t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom rather than the normal. A t of $-2.5$ says the sample mean is two and a half standard errors below the claimed mean.

blocks.name: stat-curve
blocks.cap: The t curve with 15 degrees of freedom; the shaded left tail beyond t = −2.5 is the p-value of the first example.

blocks.title: Underfilled boxes?
blocks.q: Cereal boxes are labeled 500 grams. A random sample of 16 boxes has $\bar{x} = 497.5$ g and $s = 4$ g. Test $H_0: \mu = 500$ against $H_a: \mu < 500$ at $\alpha = 0.05$.
steps: p-value: the area below $-2.5$ under the t curve with 15 df, about $0.012$ (from software).
$0.012 < 0.05$: reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that the boxes are underfilled on average.

blocks.title: A two-sided test
blocks.q: A battery maker claims a mean life of 40 hours. A random sample of 25 batteries has $\bar{x} = 41.2$ and $s = 3$. Test $H_0: \mu = 40$ against $H_a: \mu \ne 40$.
steps: $0.057 > 0.05$: fail to reject. The data do not give convincing evidence that the mean differs from 40 hours.

blocks.html: Using the normal table for t, or taking $df = n$. With 15 df, a two-sided cutoff is $2.131$, not $1.96$. Check your df and use the t distribution whenever the standard error uses $s$. And remember: "fail to reject" is not "accept."
Tests and intervals agree: a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ rejects $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ exactly when $\mu_0$ falls outside the 95% confidence interval.
